A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of modality gap, object bias, and information imbalance. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of pretrained models, controlled MAD training experiments, embedding ablations, and a numerical toy experiment.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and adds CC12M training, temperature interventions, word-frequency controls, and image-image experiments.

M1.justification: The core CLIP objective, MAD construction, and intended RMG/MOAD procedures are retained. New temperature and encoder configurations serve as experimental controls. Formula corrections and additional evaluation measures do not establish a revised proposed learning algorithm.

E1.justification: v1's controlled caption-information interventions use synthetic MAD. v2 adds natural-caption truncation experiments on CC12M and image-image matching with selectively cropped views on MS COCO (Appendices F.1 and F.4). These introduce materially different information-imbalance scenarios while retaining the original evaluation benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds a real-words baseline within the ideal-word and shifted-ideal-word comparison; v1 Section 4.3 reports only their alignment similarities. Appendix F.1 also evaluates L2I alongside RMG as an alternative gap measure. The established CLIP/SigLIP and RMG/L2M comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 filters the analytical cohort from 112 to 98 models, changes the medium-dataset cutoff from 128M to 140M, and replaces Spearman with Kendall correlations. Dimension-ablation plots use RMG instead of L2M, and Table 5 revises the stated centering treatment for shifted ideal words. New caption-length, temperature-freezing, and image-image experiments introduce additional controlled evaluation designs.

E4.justification: v2 adds caption-truncation and temperature ablations, CommonPool filtering analysis, CLIP/CLIP-A stratification, controlled word-prior experiments, and image-image/direct-embedding tests distinguishing information imbalance from loss or initialization effects. The ideal-word analysis now tests downstream accuracy. Existing MAD and dimension-ablation analyses remain, but v1 Figure 7b's caption-presence classification-accuracy panel is removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports three-seed MAD averages without correlation significance tests. v2 adds significance indicators in Table 1 and numerical p-values in Table 3 and Appendix D.2, materially expanding uncertainty assessment for central evidence. MAD's three-seed practice remains; five seeds are reported for the new image-image experiment, rather than an increase for retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial caption, entropy, filtering, word-prior, and image-image results; Table 8 reports RMG 0.006 without versus 0.149 with information imbalance. Table 5 replaces v1's CLIP/MIT-States ideal-word cosine values 0.19/0.56 with 0.388/0.858 and adds accuracies. Revised correlations and shifting procedures preclude interpreting these replacements as same-setting gains. Table 2's neighborhood distances remain identical.

T1.justification: v2 corrects RMG's matching-pair and exclusion indices, corrects the second mismatch pair in the retained toy construction, and defines L2I. The expanded MOAD and loss expressions largely restate existing mathematics. Appendix F.3 also introduces an inconsistent nonnegative coordinate restriction despite retaining solutions with negative coordinates.

C1.justification: The common-cause claim about information imbalance and the principal object-bias findings remain. However, v2 adds the connection between modality gap and logit entropy as a central abstract, introduction, and conclusion contribution. This substantially extends the claimed explanation to a functional role in representing uncertainty.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 introduces the interpretation that embedding changes associated with the gap permit entropy adjustment, distinguishing this from global temperature control and explicitly qualifying causality. Appendix D.2 adds explanations involving CLIP-A training and data filtering. v1's standalone discussion of synthetic-to-real generalization, scale, and applicability beyond contrastive models is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices F.1–F.5 document architectures, training schedules, learning rates, batches, caption truncation, initialization, and fine-tuning for the new experiments. For example, CC12M training specifies RN50, 30 epochs, and batch size 1760. Appendix E.1 explicitly supplies MOAD normalization factors. Existing MAD hyperparameters and the OpenCLIP access reference remain.

R1.justification: v2 engages Fahim et al. (2024)'s contrastive-gap explanation through replication and discussion, and adds references to language rewrites and UMAP. It removes v1's discussion connecting the work to multimodal identifiability and captioning-based representation learning. The broader positioning around information imbalance versus existing gap explanations remains.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and explanatory prose; reorders the modality-gap analyses; absorbs the former Section 4.3; and reorganizes Section 6 into two subsections. Detailed definitions and examples move into reorganized appendices, while the standalone Discussion section disappears.

P2.justification: v2 changes page format and typography, redraws the information-imbalance and MAD diagrams, reorganizes v1 Figures 3–4 into Figures 4/11, and redistributes Figure 8 across Figures 7/12. New experimental plots and Tables 3–9 substantially expand the displays. Figure 7a's new subtitle incorrectly reverses the bias trend shown by its curves and main caption.

improvement.justification: v1 Section 7 acknowledges that controlled validation relies on synthetic MAD. v2's CC12M interventions provide direct real-data evidence for the modality-gap hypothesis, while temperature and alternative-cause controls substantially strengthen its empirical explanation. Correlation p-values also improve transparency. These substantive gains outweigh the local inconsistencies introduced in Figure 7a and Appendix F.3.
